title: Golf Simulator Room Size: Ceiling Height, Width and Depth (Calculator)
metaDescription: How much space do you need for a golf simulator? Usually a 9–10 ft ceiling, 10–12 ft width (14 ft+ for lefties and righties) and 15–20 ft depth. Check your room with our calculator.
content:
For a comfortable home golf simulator, plan on a **ceiling of 9–10 ft or more**, a **width of 10–12 ft** (14 ft+ if left- and right-handers will share it) and a **depth of 15–20 ft**. Depth depends on your launch monitor: radar units that sit behind you need several extra feet.

Ceiling height is the dealbreaker in most rooms, and there's only one reliable test: **take your driver into the room and make some slow, full practice swings.** The calculator below gives you a starting point before you do.

[[tool]]

## The three measurements explained

**Ceiling height.** Most simulator guides put the minimum at **8–9 ft** with limits (shorter players, flatter swings, no driver), and the recommendation at **10 ft or more** for full driver swings and taller golfers. Our calculator uses *your height plus your driver's length* as a conservative rule of thumb. Many swings need less because the club doesn't pass straight overhead, so treat a small shortfall as a reason to swing-test, not to give up.

**Width.** With only right-handed (or only left-handed) players, you can offset the hitting mat to one side and work with **10–12 ft**. For mixed groups the mat needs to be centred, which takes **14 ft or more** to swing safely on both sides.

**Depth.** A typical layout:

| Zone | Minimum | Comfortable |
|---|---|---|
| Behind the screen (so it can flex) | ~1 ft | ~1 ft |
| Ball to screen | ~10 ft | 10–12 ft |
| Behind the ball (your swing + launch monitor) | ~4 ft | ~7 ft |
| **Total** | **~15 ft** | **18–20 ft** |

## Launch monitor placement changes the room

| Launch monitor type | Where it sits | Space impact |
|---|---|---|
| Photometric, beside the ball (e.g. SkyTrak, Bushnell) | Next to the hitting area | Standard depth works |
| Ceiling-mounted camera (e.g. Uneekor) | Overhead, ~9–10 ft up, slightly in front of the tee | Needs enough ceiling height to mount above the swing path |
| Radar behind the golfer (e.g. Garmin R10, Mevo+) | Roughly 6–10 ft behind the tee, depending on model | Adds several feet of depth |

If your room is short on depth, a side-mounted photometric unit is usually the best fit. Our [launch monitor guide](/shop/best-launch-monitors-for-golf) compares the options.

## Screen and projector

- **Screen size:** often 10–12 ft wide and 7–9 ft tall in home setups, sized to your room.
- **Projector distance:** depends on the model's throw ratio. Short-throw projectors mounted overhead avoid your shadow on the screen. See our [simulator projector guide](/shop/best-golf-sim-projector).
- **Enclosure:** a frame with side and top netting protects walls and lights from mishits. Our [enclosure guide](/shop/best-golf-enclosure) covers sizes.

## Room-by-room reality check

- **Garage:** often the best option, but check the door track and opener height, and think about heat and cold for the electronics.
- **Basement:** usually long enough, but low ceilings and beams are the common problem. Swing-test under the lowest beam.
- **Spare bedroom:** often too short and too low for full driver swings. Fine for irons, wedges and putting with a smaller screen.

Once you know the space works, our [golf simulator buying guide](/shop/best-golf-sim-buying-guide) walks through budget, launch monitor, screen and software choices.

faq.question: What ceiling height do I need for a golf simulator?
faq.answer: Aim for at least 9 ft, ideally 10 ft or more for tall players and full driver swings. Some golfers manage with 8–9 ft by limiting driver use. The only definitive test is swinging your driver in the room.

faq.question: How wide does a golf simulator room need to be?
faq.answer: About 10–12 ft for right-handed-only players with the hitting area offset, and 14 ft or more if both left- and right-handed golfers will use it with a centred hitting position.

faq.question: How deep does a golf simulator room need to be?
faq.answer: Roughly 15 ft at minimum (1 ft behind the screen, about 10 ft from ball to screen, 4 ft behind the ball) and 18–20 ft for comfort. Radar launch monitors that sit behind the golfer need more depth.

faq.question: Can I put a golf simulator in my garage?
faq.answer: Often, yes. A two-car garage is commonly about 20 × 20 ft. The usual limit is ceiling height (watch for the garage door track and opener) and temperature extremes for projectors and electronics.

title: How Far Can a Golf Cart Go on a Charge? Range Calculator + Real Numbers
metaDescription: A 48V lead-acid golf cart usually goes 15–25 miles per charge; lithium carts 30–50+. Use our range calculator to estimate your cart from voltage, amp-hours, terrain and passengers.
content:
A healthy **48 V lead-acid golf cart usually goes 15–25 miles** on a full charge. A **48 V lithium cart typically manages 30–50 miles or more**, depending on pack size. An 18-hole round is only 4–6 miles of driving, so any cart in decent shape should finish two rounds. If yours can't finish one, the batteries are the problem, not the cart.

Use the calculator below to estimate your own cart, then read on for what changes the number.

[[tool]]

## Why lithium goes so much further

It isn't magic. It comes down to how much of the battery you can safely use:

- **Lead-acid** (flooded or AGM) should only be run down to about **50%** of its rated capacity. Going deeper shortens its life sharply, and voltage sags under load.
- **Lithium (LiFePO4)** gives you about **90%** of its rating, holds voltage until it's nearly empty and weighs a fraction as much.

So a 48 V 100 Ah lithium pack (4.8 kWh) gives you more usable energy than a much "bigger" lead-acid pack. That's why it often lands in the **35–45 mile** range on flat ground.

| 48 V pack | Typical range |
|---|---|
| Lead-acid (6 × 8 V or 4 × 12 V), healthy | 15–25 miles |
| Lithium 60 Ah | 20–30 miles |
| Lithium 100–105 Ah | 35–45 miles |
| Lithium 150–160 Ah | 45–60+ miles |

## What eats your range

- **Hills:** 20–40% less range on a hilly course or neighbourhood.
- **Load:** a full 4-seater, a cargo bed or a lift kit with oversize tyres costs 10–25%.
- **Speed:** cruising at 20 mph+ costs noticeably more than 12–15 mph.
- **Tyre pressure:** soft tyres are an easy few percent lost. Check them monthly.
- **Cold:** both chemistries lose capacity in cold weather. Lithium packs often limit charging below freezing.
- **Accessories:** light bars, sound systems and heaters all draw from the same pack.
- **Age:** a 5–7-year-old lead-acid pack may only have a fraction of its original range left. Our guide on [how to tell if a golf cart battery is bad](/blog/how-to-tell-if-a-golf-cart-battery-is-bad) walks you through the tests.

## Getting more range from the cart you have

1. **Charge after every use** (lead-acid). Don't store it half-empty.
2. **Check water levels** in flooded batteries monthly and top up with distilled water after charging.
3. **Clean and tighten the terminals.** Corrosion is resistance, and resistance is wasted energy.
4. **Keep tyres at the recommended pressure**, usually printed on the sidewall.
5. **Drive smoothly.** Hard launches and constant full throttle drain any battery.
6. **If the pack is old anyway, look at lithium.** A [lithium conversion](/blog/convert-golf-cart-to-lithium-battery) usually costs less than people expect once you count a lead-acid replacement plus water, maintenance and weight. You'll also need a [lithium-compatible charger](/shop/best-golf-cart-lithium-battery-charger).

## How we estimate range

The calculator multiplies pack voltage by amp-hours to get the energy (kWh). It then applies a usable share (90% lithium, 50% lead-acid) and divides by an assumed consumption of about **120 Wh per mile** for a two-seater on flat ground at normal speeds. Terrain, passengers, lift kits and speed raise that figure. Treat the result as a planning estimate, not a guarantee.
primaryKeyword: how far can a golf cart go on a charge

faq.question: How many miles can a golf cart go on one charge?
faq.answer: Typically 15–25 miles for a 48V lead-acid cart in good health and 30–50+ miles for a 48V lithium cart, depending on pack size, terrain, load and speed.

faq.question: How many holes of golf can an electric cart play on one charge?
faq.answer: An 18-hole round usually uses 4–6 miles of driving, so a healthy cart covers 36 holes or more with plenty in reserve. If yours struggles to finish 18, the batteries are probably worn.

faq.question: Does a lithium battery really double range?
faq.answer: Often close to it, for the same size pack. Lithium lets you use about 90% of its rated capacity, while lead-acid should only be run to about 50% to avoid shortening its life, and lithium is lighter too.

faq.question: What reduces golf cart range the most?
faq.answer: Hills (often 20–40% less range), extra passengers and lift kits with big tyres (10–25%), driving at top speed, under-inflated tyres, cold weather and ageing batteries.

title: How Long Does a Round of Golf Take? 9 and 18 Holes Explained
metaDescription: An 18-hole round takes about 4 hours 10 minutes for a foursome; 9 holes about 2 hours. What changes it (group size, carts, course, tee intervals) and how to plan your day.
content:
An 18-hole round takes **about 4 hours 10 minutes** for a group of four on a typical public course. That's around **12–14 minutes per hole**. Nine holes take **about 2 hours**. On a quiet weekday a twosome can play 18 in 3–3.5 hours. On a packed Saturday it can stretch towards 5.

## Typical round times

| Group | 9 holes | 18 holes |
|---|---|---|
| Single player | ~1–1.25 h | ~2 h or less |
| Twosome | ~1.5 h | ~3–3.5 h |
| Threesome | ~1.75 h | ~3.5–4 h |
| Foursome | ~2 h | ~4–4.5 h |
| Busy weekend / event | 2.5 h+ | 4.5–5 h+ |

These assume you aren't held up. In practice **the group in front sets your pace**: a fast pair stuck behind a slow four plays at the four's speed.

## What makes a round longer

- **Tee intervals:** 7–8 minutes between groups packs the course tighter than 10–12.
- **Time and day:** weekend mornings are the busiest. Late afternoon and weekday mornings are the quickest.
- **Course design:** long walks from greens to tees, lots of water hazards and tough rough all add time.
- **Skill level:** more shots and more searching for balls. Beginners should play the forward tees and pick up when they reach their maximum score.
- **Formats:** scrambles and shotgun events often take longer than normal rounds.

## Walking or riding?

A cart saves time between shots, but it isn't a guaranteed shortcut. On **cart-path-only** days you walk back and forth to the path with clubs, and many walking foursomes keep pace with riders. Single-rider [golf scooters](/shop/best-one-person-golf-cart) are the quickest way round when the course is open ahead of you.

## How to play faster without rushing

1. **Play "ready golf"** in casual rounds: whoever is ready hits, if it's safe.
2. **Know your yardage early.** A [rangefinder or GPS](/shop/best-golf-rangefinder-under-200-budget-buying-guide) beats pacing off sprinkler heads.
3. **Line up putts while others putt** instead of starting when it's your turn.
4. **Leave bags and carts on the side of the green nearest the next tee.**
5. **Limit ball searches** to the three minutes the Rules allow.
6. **Have a [packed bag](/shop/golf-bag-checklist)** so nobody holds things up looking for tees or a glove.

## Planning your day

Allow about **5–5.5 hours** door to door for 18 holes: arrive 30 minutes early to check in and warm up, then add time for the drive and a drink afterwards. For 9 holes after work, two and a half hours is a safe estimate.
primaryKeyword: how long does a game of golf last

faq.question: How long does 18 holes of golf take?
faq.answer: About 4 hours 10 minutes for a foursome on a typical public course; roughly 3.5 hours on a quick day and close to 5 hours on a busy weekend.

faq.question: How long does 9 holes of golf take?
faq.answer: Usually about 2 hours for a foursome, often 1.5 hours or less for a twosome or a single player on a quiet course.

faq.question: Is golf faster with a cart?
faq.answer: Usually a little, because you get to your ball faster, but the group ahead sets the real pace. Cart-path-only days after rain can make riding slower than walking.

faq.question: How long does a round take for one person?
faq.answer: Two hours or less for 18 holes if the course is empty ahead of you. If you catch up with a slower group, you'll play at their pace unless they let you through.

title: What Is a Golf Stick Called? Golf Clubs Explained for Beginners
metaDescription: A golf 'stick' is called a golf club. Here are the types (driver, woods, hybrids, irons, wedges, putter), what each is for, the parts of a club and the 14-club limit.
content:
The "stick" you hit a golf ball with is called a **golf club**. Golfers carry a set of different clubs, up to **14** under the Rules of Golf, because each one hits the ball a different height and distance.

(If you meant the tall stick with a flag on the green, that's the **flagstick**, or "pin".)

## The types of golf clubs

| Club | What it's for | Typical loft |
|---|---|---|
| **Driver** | Longest club, used off the tee on long holes | ~8–12° |
| **Fairway woods** (3-, 5-wood) | Long shots from the tee or fairway | ~15–19° |
| **Hybrids** | Easier-to-hit replacements for long irons | ~17–28° |
| **Irons** (typically 4–9) | Approach shots. Lower number = longer, lower flight | ~20–42° |
| **Wedges** (pitching, gap, sand, lob) | Short approaches, chips, bunker shots | ~44–60°+ |
| **Putter** | Rolling the ball into the hole on the green | ~2–4° |

"Loft" is the angle of the clubface. More loft sends the ball higher and shorter.

## Parts of a golf club

- **Grip:** the rubber handle you hold.
- **Shaft:** the long tube, usually steel for irons and graphite for drivers and woods. Its stiffness is called its **flex**.
- **Clubhead:** the part that hits the ball. Its face has **grooves** on irons and wedges.
- **Hosel:** where the shaft joins the head. Many drivers have an adjustable hosel to change loft.

Drivers have limits too: the clubhead can't exceed 460 cc. There's more in our [driver head size guide](/shop/golf-driver-head-size-guide).

## What a beginner actually needs

You don't need 14 clubs to start. A half set covers almost everything:

- Driver or 3-wood
- 1 hybrid
- 7-iron and 9-iron
- Sand or pitching wedge
- Putter

Complete boxed sets are an affordable way to get all of that in one go. See our [Callaway Edge set review](/shop/callaway-edge-womens-golf-set-review) for an example of what's included. Before your first round, run through our [golf bag checklist](/shop/golf-bag-checklist).

## Other golf words you'll hear

- **Tee:** the peg you rest the ball on for your first shot on a hole, and also the area you hit from.
- **Fairway:** the short grass between the tee and the green.
- **Green:** the very short grass around the hole, where you putt.
- **Par:** the number of shots a good player is expected to take on a hole.
- **Handicap:** a measure of your ability that lets players of different levels compete. Try our [handicap calculator](/shop/golf-handicap-calculator).
primaryKeyword: what is a golf stick called

faq.question: What is the golf stick called?
faq.answer: A golf club. Each club has a grip, a shaft and a clubhead; the different types are driver, fairway woods, hybrids, irons, wedges and putter.

faq.question: How many clubs are in a golf bag?
faq.answer: Up to 14 are allowed under the Rules of Golf. A typical set is a driver, one or two fairway woods or hybrids, irons from about 5 to 9, two to four wedges and a putter.

faq.question: What is the stick on the green called?
faq.answer: That is the flagstick (or 'pin'), which marks the hole. You may leave it in or take it out when putting.

title: What Is a Good Golf Score? Averages, Benchmarks and Is 85 Good?
metaDescription: The average US golfer shoots about 94 for 18 holes. About 26% break 90 and 5% break 80. See where your score sits, whether 85 is good, and targets for beginners.
content:
For an adult recreational golfer, **breaking 100 is a solid score, breaking 90 is good and breaking 80 is excellent.** The average US golfer shoots **about 94** for 18 holes, according to the USGA. Only **about 26%** of adult golfers average under 90, and **about 5%** average under 80.

So yes, **85 is a good score**. If that's your normal round, you're ahead of roughly three out of four golfers.

## Where your score sits

| Typical 18-hole score | Share of adult golfers who average better | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Under 70 | under 2% | Elite amateur / plus handicap |
| Under 80 | ~5% | Excellent, single-digit territory |
| Under 90 | ~26% | Good, a solid club golfer |
| Under 100 | ~55% | Respectable, the first big milestone |
| 100+ | ~45% | Most beginners and occasional players |

Percentages are based on National Golf Foundation data for scores people *typically* shoot, not their best-ever round.

## Score vs handicap

Scores depend on the course. 85 on a long, tight championship course is a better round than 85 on a short resort course. That's why golf uses the **Handicap Index**, which adjusts each score for course difficulty using the course rating and slope.

The USGA puts the average Handicap Index at **14.2 for men** and **28.7 for women**. Plug a few of your scores into our [handicap calculator](/shop/golf-handicap-calculator) to see where you land.

Rough guide on an average-difficulty course (rating ~71, slope ~125), assuming your best rounds are 2–3.5 strokes better than your average:

| Average score | Approx. Handicap Index |
|---|---|
| 75 | ~0–2 |
| 80 | ~5–6 |
| 85 | ~9–11 |
| 90 | ~14–15 |
| 95 | ~18–20 |
| 100 | ~23–24 |

Because your index uses your *best* recent rounds, it usually comes out a few strokes lower than your average score suggests.

## Good targets by experience

- **First season:** finish holes without a time limit and post scores. 110–120 is normal at first.
- **Year one to two:** break 100. Most of the gain comes from fewer penalty shots and three-putts.
- **Regular golfer:** break 90. Typically means hitting more greens from 150 yards in and getting up and down occasionally.
- **Keen club golfer:** break 80. Needs consistent ball-striking and a reliable short game.

## The fastest ways to lower your score

1. **Stop the big numbers.** Take your medicine after a bad shot and chip back to the fairway. One triple bogey ruins a card more than three bogeys.
2. **Count your putts.** Most mid-handicappers lose more strokes to three-putts than to drives. Practise speed from 30–40 ft.
3. **Play the right tees.** Too far back turns par 4s into par 5s.
4. **Track simple stats:** fairways, greens, putts and penalties. Our [guide to lowering your handicap](/blog/how-to-lower-your-golf-handicap) shows what to do with them.
primaryKeyword: what is a good golf score

faq.question: What is the average golf score for 18 holes?
faq.answer: About 94 for US golfers, according to USGA figures based on National Golf Foundation data. The average Handicap Index is 14.2 for men and 28.7 for women.

faq.question: Is 85 a good golf score?
faq.answer: Yes. Averaging around 85 puts you ahead of roughly three-quarters of adult golfers, since only about 26% average under 90. It typically corresponds to a Handicap Index of roughly 9–11, depending on the course.

faq.question: Is 100 a good score for a beginner?
faq.answer: Yes. Breaking 100 is the first big milestone; about 55% of adult golfers average under 100, so a beginner who gets there in the first season or two is doing well.

faq.question: What percentage of golfers break 80?
faq.answer: Only about 5% of adult golfers average under 80, and fewer than 2% break 70 with any regularity.

title: What Is My Handicap If I Shoot 100? (Worked Examples)
metaDescription: If you regularly shoot 100, your Handicap Index will usually land around 22–26, depending on course rating and slope. Worked examples and a calculator to check your own.
content:
If 100 is your normal score, your Handicap Index will usually land **somewhere around 22–26**. The exact number depends on the **course rating and slope** of the courses you play and on how much your scores vary. The handicap system averages your *best* rounds, so the occasional 94 pulls your index down more than a bad 108 pushes it up.

## Worked examples: a score of 100 on different courses

Differential = (100 − course rating) × 113 ÷ slope

| Course | Rating / slope | Differential for a 100 |
|---|---|---|
| Short, easy municipal | 68.0 / 113 | 32.0 |
| Average parkland course | 71.0 / 125 | 26.2 |
| Tougher course | 72.5 / 135 | 23.0 |
| Championship tees | 74.5 / 145 | 19.9 |

The same 100 is worth very different amounts. Shooting 100 from the championship tees of a hard course is a better round than 92 on an easy one.

## From differentials to your index

Say your last 20 rounds were all on an average course (71.0 / 125), mostly around 100, with a few good days:

- Best 8 scores: 93, 94, 95, 95, 96, 96, 97, 97
- Their differentials: 19.9, 20.8, 21.7, 21.7, 22.6, 22.6, 23.5, 23.5
- Average: **22.0**, so your **Handicap Index is 22.0**

Same golfer, same average score, but the index reflects the good days. That's by design: it measures your potential, not your average.

## Try it with your own scores

[[tool]]

## Getting from 100 to the 90s

At this level the quickest gains rarely come from swing changes:

1. **Cut penalty shots.** Use a club you can keep in play off the tee, even if it's a hybrid.
2. **Avoid the second chip.** Get every chip onto the green, even if it finishes 20 ft away.
3. **Lag putts.** Aim to leave every long putt inside a 3-ft circle. Three-putts are the hidden killer at the 100 level.
4. **Play the right tees** for your distance.

There's more in our guides on [lowering your handicap](/blog/how-to-lower-your-golf-handicap) and [what counts as a good score](/shop/what-is-a-good-golf-score).
primaryKeyword: what is my golf handicap if i shoot 100

faq.question: What handicap is a golfer who shoots 100?
faq.answer: Typically a Handicap Index of about 22–26. On an average course (rating ~71, slope ~125) a 100 produces a differential of about 26; because your index uses your best rounds, regular 100-shooters with a few better days usually end up in the low-to-mid 20s.

faq.question: Is a 100 golf score bad?
faq.answer: No. Roughly 45% of adult golfers average 100 or more, and breaking 100 is the first real milestone for most players.

faq.question: What handicap do I need to break 90?
faq.answer: Consistently breaking 90 usually corresponds to a Handicap Index in the mid-teens or lower, depending on the courses you play.

title: Golf Cart Clutch Problems: Drive vs Driven Clutch, Symptoms and Repair Costs
metaDescription: Gas golf cart slipping, juddering or revving without moving? How the drive and driven clutches work, which symptoms point where, belt checks and typical repair costs ($200–$800 installed).
content:
Gas golf carts use a **CVT**: a **drive clutch** on the engine and a **driven clutch** on the axle, linked by a belt. When the cart **revs but barely moves, judders on take-off, struggles on hills or smells of hot rubber**, the problem is almost always the **belt or one of the two clutches**. Check the belt first: it's the cheapest fix. Clutch repairs typically run **$200–$800 installed**.

Electric carts don't have this system. This guide is for gas carts only.

## How the two clutches work

- **Drive (primary) clutch, on the engine:** stays open at idle. As RPM rises, weights push its sheaves together, gripping the belt and pushing it outward. Think of it as shifting into a taller gear.
- **Driven (secondary) clutch, on the axle:** spring-loaded, it opens and closes in response. It also lets the system shift back down when you climb or slow down.

They work as a pair, so a problem in one often shows up as wear on the belt.

## Symptom → likely cause

| Symptom | Most likely |
|---|---|
| Engine revs high, cart moves slowly | Worn or glazed belt, or drive clutch not closing properly |
| Jerky, grabbing take-off | Dirty or worn drive clutch, idle set too high |
| Poor hill climbing | Driven clutch spring or ramp wear, worn belt |
| Slow to pick up after you ease off | Driven clutch sticking (dirt, wear) |
| Rattle or wobble from the engine side | Worn drive clutch bushings or weights |
| Squeal, burning smell, heavy black dust | Slipping belt, misalignment, worn clutch faces |

## Check the belt first

Remove it and look for **cracks, missing chunks, frayed edges or shiny, glazed sides**. A belt that has worn narrow sits lower in the pulleys and slips. Use the correct belt for your model and year. Belts are inexpensive and often fix the problem on their own.

## Cleaning and maintenance

- **Clean the sheaves dry.** Belt dust builds up and causes erratic engagement. Use a brush, compressed air or a residue-free cleaner.
- **Don't oil the belt faces.** Any lubricant where the belt runs causes slipping. Only lubricate parts your service manual names.
- **Check alignment.** Misaligned clutches wear belts fast. Engine swap guides warn that more than about 1/8 inch of misalignment causes vibration and rapid belt wear.
- **Inspect regularly.** A common recommendation is to check the belt and clutches **every six months or ~125 hours**, more often on dusty roads.

## Typical costs

| Job | Cost |
|---|---|
| Inspection / cleaning | $50–$150 |
| Drive belt | $20–$120 DIY, $90–$250 installed |
| Clutch puller tool | $15–$35 |
| Aftermarket clutch | $80–$300 |
| OEM / premium clutch | $250–$600 |
| Installed clutch repair | $200–$800 |

## Upgrades and engine swaps

If you've fitted a bigger engine, the stock clutch usually isn't up to it, which is why [engine swap kits](/shop/best-golf-cart-engine-swap) include a matched clutch. Higher-rated springs and weights can also change how the cart accelerates and climbs. Change one thing at a time and test.

If the cart revs and the clutch engages but it still loses power on hills, the issue may be fuel delivery. See our [EZGO fuel pump guide](/shop/ezgo-golf-cart-fuel-pump-diagram-guide).

faq.question: What are the symptoms of a bad golf cart clutch?
faq.answer: The engine revs but the cart barely moves, a jerky or grabbing take-off, juddering or rattling from the clutch area, poor hill climbing, slow recovery after you ease off, squealing or a burning-rubber smell and lots of belt dust.

faq.question: How much does it cost to fix a golf cart clutch?
faq.answer: Roughly $200–$800 installed. Aftermarket clutches run about $80–$300 and OEM or premium ones $250–$600; a new drive belt is $20–$120 to buy or $90–$250 installed.

faq.question: Is it the clutch or the belt?
faq.answer: Check the belt first: cracks, missing chunks, glazed shiny sides or a belt that sits too low in the pulleys all cause slipping. If a new belt doesn't fix it, look at the clutches.

faq.question: Should I lubricate my golf cart clutch?
faq.answer: Not the faces where the belt runs; oil or spray there causes slipping. Clean the sheaves with a dry brush or a cleaner that leaves no residue, and only lubricate parts the service manual specifies.

title: Golf Cart Charger Not Working? Step-by-Step Fixes for EZGO, Club Car and Yamaha
metaDescription: Golf cart charger won't turn on or stops early? Check the outlet, pack voltage (most 48V chargers need ~30V to start), fuses and receptacle, then read the error lights. Brand-specific tips inside.
content:
When a golf cart charger won't start, the cause is usually something simple: **the outlet, a pack so flat the charger can't detect it, a blown fuse or a corroded receptacle.** Work through the steps below in order. Most fixes cost nothing or a few dollars, so check everything before you replace a $300–$600 charger.

Use a multimeter, work with the cart switched off and keep metal tools away from battery terminals.

## Step 1: power at the wall

- Plug a lamp or phone charger into the same outlet. Does it work?
- Reset any tripped **GFCI** outlet or breaker.
- Avoid long or thin extension cords. They can drop the voltage enough to stop the charger.

## Step 2: is the pack too flat?

Most chargers need to "see" a minimum pack voltage before they start. On a **48 V system that's roughly 30 V**. Measure across the main pack terminals:

- **Below the threshold:** the charger thinks no battery is connected. See our [guide to charging a dead golf cart battery](/blog/how-to-charge-a-dead-golf-cart-battery) for safe ways to bring it back.
- **Normal voltage but still no charge:** carry on.

A pack that keeps falling this low usually has a [failing battery](/blog/how-to-tell-if-a-golf-cart-battery-is-bad), or something on the cart drains it in storage.

## Step 3: fuses, receptacle and cord

- **Cart-side fuse:** many carts have a fuse between the charging receptacle and the pack. A blown fuse stops charging even though everything else looks fine.
- **Receptacle:** look for burnt, loose or corroded pins. Heat damage here is common and worth fixing quickly.
- **DC cord:** check the charger's output cord for cuts and test it for continuity.

## Step 4: brand-specific checks

**E-Z-GO (PowerWise / Delta-Q based chargers).** Watch the LED when you plug in. Common flash codes include **1 = battery voltage too high, 2 = too low, 3 = charge timeout, 4 = battery temperature too high, 6 = internal fault**. A timeout often points to a weak battery rather than a bad charger.

**Club Car (OBC carts, roughly 1995–2014).** These use an on-board computer that controls charging. It can sometimes be reset by disconnecting the main negative battery cable with the cart in neutral, waiting, then reconnecting. Follow the exact steps in your manual, as procedures differ by model.

**Yamaha.** Listen for a relay **click a few seconds after plugging in**. No click, with good voltage and a working outlet, suggests a relay or control-board problem in the charger or cart.

## Step 5: charger or batteries?

- The charger starts and then **stops after a few minutes:** often a bad battery or a poor connection. Test each battery.
- It **runs forever** without finishing: a battery may have a failed cell, or the charger isn't regulating.
- **Nothing at all** after all the checks above: the charger is the likely culprit. Get it bench-tested if a local shop offers it.

## Switching to lithium?

Lead-acid chargers aren't a safe match for most lithium packs. Use a [lithium-compatible charger](/shop/best-golf-cart-lithium-battery-charger) with the correct profile. Our [golf cart charger guide](/shop/best-golf-cart-battery-charger) covers what to buy.

faq.question: Why won't my golf cart charger turn on?
faq.answer: Most often the battery pack is too flat for the charger to detect (around 30V on a 48V system), the wall outlet or GFCI has tripped, a fuse on the cart side has blown, or the charging receptacle is corroded. Less often, the charger itself has failed.

faq.question: How do I charge a golf cart battery that is too dead to charge?
faq.answer: Bring the pack voltage up enough for the charger to recognise it, either by charging the batteries individually with a suitable charger or by following the safe procedure in our dead-battery guide. Then charge the pack normally and test each battery.

faq.question: What do the flashing lights on an EZGO charger mean?
faq.answer: On Delta-Q based chargers used by E-Z-GO, flash codes indicate faults: for example 1 flash for battery voltage too high, 2 for too low, 3 for a charge timeout, 4 for high battery temperature and 6 for an internal charger fault. Check your charger's manual, as codes vary by model.

faq.question: Can I use my old charger with new lithium batteries?
faq.answer: Only if it has a matching lithium charge profile or the battery maker approves it. Lead-acid chargers can undercharge or overcharge lithium packs, so use a lithium-compatible charger.

title: How Much Does a Golf Simulator Cost? Budget, Mid-Range and Premium Builds
metaDescription: A home golf simulator costs from under $1,000 (launch monitor, net and mat) to $2,000–$4,000 for a starter sim, $5,000–$10,000 mid-range and $10,000–$20,000+ premium. Full cost breakdown.
content:
A home golf simulator can cost **under $1,000 or well over $20,000**. Realistic tiers:

- **Practice setup** (launch monitor, net, mat): **~$700–$1,500**
- **Starter simulator** (adds screen, enclosure, budget projector): **~$2,000–$4,000**
- **Mid-range** (better launch monitor, short-throw projector, premium mat): **~$5,000–$10,000**
- **Premium** (high-end photometric or overhead launch monitor, laser projector): **~$10,000–$20,000+**

The **launch monitor** is the biggest single cost and the hardest thing to upgrade later, so that's where to spend first.

## Cost breakdown by tier

| Component | Practice | Starter | Mid-range | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Launch monitor | ~$600 | $600–$700 | ~$3,000 | $7,000–$10,000+ |
| Net or screen | Net $100–$200 | Screen + enclosure $800–$1,200 | Screen $400–$600 + enclosure $800–$1,500 | Pro-grade screen and enclosure |
| Hitting mat | $150–$300 | $150–$300 | ~$600 | Premium mat |
| Projector | Phone/tablet | $500–$700 | $1,200–$2,000 short-throw | $2,000–$5,000 laser |
| **Typical total** | **$700–$1,500** | **$2,000–$4,000** | **$5,000–$10,000** | **$10,000–$20,000+** |

Examples at each level include radar units such as the Garmin Approach R10 or Rapsodo MLM2Pro at the entry level, photometric units like the Bushnell Launch Pro or SkyTrak+ mid-range, and Foresight or Uneekor systems at the top. Prices change often. Our [launch monitor guide](/shop/best-launch-monitors-for-golf) compares the options.

## Costs people forget

- **Software:** many launch monitors need a subscription for full course play and features, typically **$100–$200 a year**.
- **Computer or tablet:** some simulator software needs a capable PC for good graphics.
- **Room preparation:** flooring, electrics, lighting and sometimes moving a garage door opener, **~$500–$2,000**.
- **Replacement parts:** mats wear where you hit, and screens eventually need replacing.
- **Installation:** optional, but common for enclosures and ceiling-mounted projectors.

## Where to spend and where to save

1. **Launch monitor first.** Accurate ball and club data is the point of the whole setup. A cheap screen with a good monitor beats the reverse.
2. **The mat matters for your joints.** A poor mat bounces the club and hurts wrists and elbows. Spend more here than you'd expect.
3. **Save on the enclosure.** DIY frames and netting work well if you're handy.
4. **Projector last.** Start with a TV or tablet and add a projector once you know you'll use the sim.

## Check the room before you buy

Ceiling height and depth decide which launch monitors and screens will work. Run your numbers through our [golf simulator room size calculator](/shop/golf-simulator-room-size) before you order anything.

faq.question: How much does a home golf simulator cost?
faq.answer: A basic practice setup (launch monitor, net and mat) can cost under $1,000. A starter simulator with a screen, enclosure and budget projector is typically $2,000–$4,000; mid-range builds $5,000–$10,000; premium builds $10,000–$20,000 and up.

faq.question: What is the most expensive part of a golf simulator?
faq.answer: The launch monitor, by a wide margin, from about $600 for entry-level radar units to $7,000–$10,000+ for premium photometric or overhead camera systems.

faq.question: Are there ongoing costs?
faq.answer: Usually software subscriptions of roughly $100–$200 a year for course play and features, plus occasional screen, mat and projector lamp replacement. Room preparation (flooring, electrical, lighting) can add $500–$2,000 up front.

faq.question: What's the cheapest way to start?
faq.answer: Buy the best launch monitor you can afford and pair it with a net and a good mat. Add the screen, enclosure and projector later; the launch monitor is the part that's hardest to upgrade cheaply.
